item.title: People Should Resolve Tensions In AI Safety Research
item.description:
By now, there are lots of AI safety research papers, more than what is reasonable for a single person to read. This will get worse as the machines get better at AI safety research, and as more talent and resources pour into the field. But the "paper" is an arbitrary unit, we really care about if we make progress on an "uncertainty" or an "issue", which papers provide heterogeneous and sometimes contradictory evidence towards. Right now, I loosely claim that we should have more short writeups that simply compile evidence from papers (particularly contradictory evidence), and reconcile them into an answer for a question.

Why?

  1. Object level, it's good for the field.
    1. It's hard to sift through all these papers! Organising them is useful and saves time.
    2. Orienting towards research questions is a good way to organise our understanding so that we can productively identify gaps and write papers. This was partly what motivated Stress-Testing Alignment Midtraining.
    3. Interesting progress comes out of contradictions, where people have differing intuitions and experimental results. Methodological errors can also be exposed if we have two things that should be the same, but are actually different.
  2. It's good for field-building reasons.
    1. It's probably better than the average experiment cooked up by a person + Claude. And, it's cheaper to fail here.
    2. Most people probably read too few papers, so this could also improve the average experiment done by someone, as a forced related work.
    3. The writeups themselves are more likely to be accessible to newcomers when it comes to understanding important questions in the field.

It's worth it for people at a variety of seniority levels to do this, not just very new people. But for more senior people, this tends to look something like laying out a research agenda anyway.

Here's a (rushed, not great) example:

  1. Does reward hacking learned from RL also cause emergent misalignment?
    1. Although I think this question became quite prominent from MacDiarmid et al. (2025), I view it as arising from Denison et al. (2024), which tested whether models that had learned low-level specification gaming would generalize to the more serious reward tampering when given the chance. They found that it was quite rare. The original EM paper then described EM as distinct from reward hacking and sycophancy, citing Denison et al.
    2. This question is significant because there's tons of reward hacking (to some degree due to sloppy RL environments ).
  2. Evidence for
    • MacDiarmid et al. (2025): misalignment jumped on all evals the moment the model learned to hack. But, the main caveat IMO is that the hacks were primed by synthetic documents or prompts.
    • Jose & Stastny (2026): independent replication of the above on Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct with GRPO. Misalignment rose once hacking started, and runs that never hacked showed no increase. Inoculation prompting blocked it. Again, there were hack hints in prompt.
    • Taylor et al. (2025): 12% misaligned responses vs 0% for baselines. But, this was in SFT, not RL, so this is proxy evidence for the question.
    • Daniels et al. (2026): GPT-4.1 showed covert power-seeking and alignment faking after iterative DPO. This didn’t have synthetic docs or hints, though the task prompts state their own grading criteria, which may make the exploits salient in a similar way. It’s also iterative DPO rather than "full RL", though, the authors appeal to previous work showing iterative DPO approximates GRPO.
    • Jørgenvåg et al. (2026): This isn't reward hacking (since the grader openly rewards bad behaviour, so it's arguably in the spirit of the task) but it's relevant to how much we should discount SFT evidence. Here, GRPO produced much more general misalignment than sample-matched SFT, but only did so after some SFT warmup; from scratch, it produced essentially none. So SFT may understate the effect in RL, but when there is misalignment, RL seems to amplify it.
  3. Evidence against (or weak)
    • Qi et al. (Anthropic, 2026), “Hacker-Opus”. This, IMO, is pretty decisive evidence on an early Opus 4.8 checkpoint with real hackable production environments, and no synthetic documents or hints. It hacked on 40% of episodes! But, it got 0% on all of MacDiarmid et al.’s EM evals, and was as aligned as the starting checkpoint when there was no grader.
    • Yudelson et al. (2026): This is also clear evidence: it's RL only, on Kimi and GPT-OSS, where similarly, hacking generalized, but EM evals stayed near zero.
    • Golechha et al. (2026). The AISI gang primed the hacks with synthetic docs or hints and got consistent hacking. But EM was inconsistent and came mostly from two evals (monitor disruption and framing a colleague). So priming doesn’t seem sufficient on its own, at least on smaller open models.
    • OpenAI’s metagaming work (2026): in a frontier training run, no misaligned persona and no misbehavior on two of MacDiarmid et al.’s evals. One caveat here is that the model didn't really learn to hack often.
    • Wang et al. (2025): coding reward hacking caused no broad EM, despite seeing increases in deception and oversight sabotage.
    • Taylor et al. ablation: coding-only hacks produced almost no EM.
  4. There is also evidence from Qi et al, Yudelson et al. and Daniels et al. that it generalises to new forms of reward hacking or reward seeking.
    • Qi et al., Yudelson et al. and Daniels et al. all find that hacking generalises to new forms of reward hacking or reward seeking.
    • This can be severe. Hacker-Opus tampered with its own reward 41% of the time, gave harmful answers to satisfy a grader 29% of the time, and attacked infrastructure in simulated cyber evals. It only did this when there was a grader or score in play.
    • This closes the loop with Denison et al.: reward tampering was rare in 2024, and here it’s 41%. So, it's gotten more common as models have gotten better, more RL'd, or something else.
  5. In terms of complications:
    • Inoculation prompting removes the generalization (MacDiarmid et al., Jose & Stastny). But, AISI saw no clear benefit from it.
    • Synthetic documents framing hacking as acceptable still didn’t prevent EM. Those models ended up more misaligned than prompted ones (Jose & Stastny).
    • Hacker-Opus was highly eval-aware on the EM evals. By now it seems the agentic scenarios are too contrived to be reliable.
    • Judges give some false positives on open models (AISI).
  6. How should we resolve this tension:
    • The starting checkpoint is important. Qi et al think this mattered a lot: their earlier work started from a base model, while Hacker-Opus started from a checkpoint that had already had alignment training.
    • Priming also matters. EM appears with synthetic documents or hints (MacDiarmid, AISI, Jose & Stastny) and is absent without them (Hacker-Opus, Yudelson). Daniels et al. seems to be kind of a counterexample to both here but:
      • GPT-4.1 is an aligned production model, so Daniels kind of messes with the starting-checkpoint story too.
      • Daniels et al. cite prior work showing iterative DPO approximates GRPO. Their DPO checkpoints also generalized to agentic reward hacking where the SFT checkpoints didn’t.
      • In general, I think that the task prompts stating their own grading criteria, is a kind of salience, and the tasks are mostly single-turn non-code ones.
    • Hack diversity is another candidate here. For example: Hacker-Opus trained on 80 hacks. Taylor et al. needed diverse, non-coding hacks to get EM. Meanwhile, Yudelson et al. used more varied hacks than the AISI replication and got none.
    • Reasoning training might be crucial here (h/t Oliver Daniels). Setups that started from a model without dedicated reasoning training got EM (MacDiarmid et al. (base model), Jose & Stastny (Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct), and Daniels et al. (GPT-4.1, and according to a comment below, Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507 in forthcoming work). On the other hand, setups starting from reasoning models got little or none: Hacker-Opus, Yudelson et al.’s on GPT-OSS and Kimi, OpenAI’s result, and AISI’s GPT-OSS runs.
      • It can’t be the whole story, though. GPT-OSS and Kimi do become emergently misaligned from SFT (Yudelson et al.), so this would have to be specific to learning hacks on-policy. Speculatively, perhaps reasoning models often rationalise hacks as intended, which may act like self-inoculation.
  7. So the answer here is:
    • In terms of persona-style EM, you only really get EM reliably when hacking is primed or the start model is weakly aligned. If the model is aligned and unprimed, you don't really get EM (except in the case of Daniels et al). This could also be disambiguated by if the model has reasoning training.
    • In terms of broader reward seeking: yes, you seem to get it consistently, and it can be severe.
    • There's a missing matched experiment here, as suggested by Claude: {base vs aligned start} × {primed vs unprimed}, on the same environments. Although in general we should score this on both the standard EM evals and probes for conditional misalignment.

This was written with the intent of being simple and accessible, so it may miss some nuance, with the assistance of Claude Opus 5.5 in collecting papers and directing my attention to experiments.

item.title: Efficient Lempel-Ziv Prediction with the Run-Length BWT
item.description:
The Lempel-Ziv parse of Chad Gadya (חד גדיא), right-to-left, drawn as an arc diagram. Generated by Claude Opus 5.5

I have published a new paper on efficient string prediction. It was written during the PIBBSS 2026 summer fellowship, under the mentorship of Vanessa Kosoy.

This research builds on Kosoy's previous work in stringology. Kosoy built a polynomial-time algorithm for predicting repetitive sequences and I have used other algorithmic techniques to further decrease the runtime.

The goal of this post is to explain some of the ideas from Kosoy's paper and how my work builds on them. My writing will be mostly informal; the field of string algorithms has a lot of technical jargon which I will not try to fully explain. I hope to mostly communicate interesting ideas and topics I've bumped into during the research, while linking to external resources for anyone who wishes to learn more.

The prediction trinity

There are three things we want every good predictor to have:

  • Power: can predict general, real-world patterns.
  • Efficiency: can run in practice.
  • Formal guarantees: we can prove what it can or can't do.

Unfortunately, no framework today satisfies all three properties at once.

Deep learning is powerful and efficient, but lacks a strong framework of formal guarantees. (This might be a problem!)

Solomonoff induction / AIXI are extremely powerful, and have formal guarantees, but can't actually run in practice.

My research is on the third edge: efficient algorithms with formal guarantees, though ones that are still not powerful enough for "actual" intelligence.

Of course, classical learning theory already has plenty of efficient algorithms with provable guarantees (e.g. linear regression). However, these algorithms assume the shape of the hypothesis is fixed in advance and learn its numerical parameters; our algorithms learn compositional structure, as described in Kosoy's compositional learning theory. (Deep learning also learns numerical parameters, but it uses them to represent hidden structure in opaque ways, while our goal is to make such structure explicit.)

The question is then: which structural prediction tasks can be done efficiently?

The hypothesis space given to Solomonoff induction is extremely ambitious: the environments are generated by any computer program. Solomonoff induction is thus uncomputable and can never be implemented in practice.

We could reduce to bounded-time programs, but it's still too expensive: going over all programs of length that run in time takes time to run. We want prediction time that is at most polynomial in the string's complexity . For that to work, we need a weaker notion of complexity than program length.

So we will work with a very specialized subset of computer programs, called straight-line programs. Straight-line programs (SLPs) are programs that have two types of instructions:

  • : assign a single symbol to a variable. ( is a general alphabet but you can think of as an example)
  • : define a new string as a concatenation of two previous ones ().

An SLP defines strings in order. The final variable is the program's output, and (the number of instructions) is called the size of the program.

We define the Straight-Line Complexity of a string , , to be the size of the smallest SLP that generates .

We write for the length of a string . We always have : we initialize variables for all symbols in the alphabet, then build the string one symbol at a time by concatenating the next symbol each instruction.

For special strings we can do much better. For example, we can build the Fibonacci words [1] by concatenating the two previous words at each step:

The lengths of follow the Fibonacci sequence. grows exponentially in the number of instructions , so these words have very short descriptions: .

Matching the string's history

An important property of small SLPs is that the strings they generate tend to be very repetitive. If a small number of instructions is used to generate a large string , it means that the variables in the program appear over and over again when constructing .

For example, expanding the definition of the Fibonacci word results in two occurrences of and three occurrences of : (they actually appear more than that if you look at the boundaries between different terms)

We can use that insight for prediction: when predicting the next symbol, we look at the last few symbols, search for all previous occurrences of this string, and return the symbol that followed them most often.

If we take a partial version of : , we see that the last 4 digits have two previous occurrences in the string [2] , and each such occurrence was followed by a 0. This correctly predicts that the last digit of is 0.

The idea of "match the last few symbols" is formalized by the Lempel-Ziv factorization of (optional technical explanation given below).

Lempel-Ziv factorization

Lempel-Ziv (LZ77) is a string processing algorithm that decomposes a string into repeating components. The Lempel-Ziv phrases are defined inductively: is either a single symbol (if that's its first occurrence in ), or the longest prefix of that has an earlier occurrence in . is defined as the number of phrases in the Lempel-Ziv decomposition of .

The prediction algorithms described in this post are proved in terms of and not . This suffices for predicting strings generated by small SLPs, because we can show that in general.

Lempel-Ziv Plurality (LZP) uses the last Lempel-Ziv phrase as its context and predicts the symbol that most often followed its earlier occurrences.

LZP has two operations:

  • predict: Output the predicted next symbol,
  • update: Process the actual next symbol after it is revealed.

In her paper, Kosoy proves the following result:

Theorem (Kosoy): Assume a constant-size alphabet and let be a string with . Then LZP predicts with at most mistakes. A single update and prediction costs .

Now we have an algorithm that runs in polynomial time in terms of the string's complexity !

Going faster

What are the conceptual inner workings of LZP? What is it bottlenecked by? Can we make it faster?

LZP provides a reduction: from predicting the future ("what is the next symbol?"), to querying the past ("how often did this substring appear before?"). The problem of string matching is widely studied, and for example, computational biologists use it all the time when searching for short DNA sequences within a genome.

Kosoy uses a data structure by Kempa and Kociumaka called -SA, which takes a compressed Lempel-Ziv representation of a string and "indexes" it to make pattern matching on much faster. The problem is that it's a static structure: once we get the new symbol , we have to throw away the index we built for and build a new one for . The amazing property of -SA is that its construction is fast for repetitive strings: the time complexity is , which is polynomial in and not in (which can be much larger).

Still, we would like a dynamic structure here.

For this purpose, I use a different string-processing technique called the Burrows-Wheeler Transform.

I won't get into the technical details here - see here for a great series of lectures on BWT.

The TL;DR is that instead of saving the string in memory, we save a certain permutation of it, called . This permutation has two great properties:

Fast string search: The occurrences of a string inside match a contiguous interval . To find the number of occurrences of in (where is a candidate next symbol), [3] we just have to count the number of occurrences of in . This can be calculated by two rank queries: , where is the number of occurrences of in . [4]

Compressed form: For repetitive strings , consists of a small number of long runs of the same symbol. This allows us to write much more succinctly, taking less space. This is called the Run-Length representation of BWT, and denoted RLBWT (not to be confused with the other type of RL).

Here's an example adapted from Langmead's lectures:

has 64 symbols but only has runs.

It can be shown that in general, so a string with small straight-line complexity will also have a short RLBWT representation.

We can implement dynamic RLBWT with efficient update and rank operations: both cost time, where is the number of runs in . By the statement above, this is time.

Using this construction, we get a predictor that:

  • Updates in time ,
  • Predicts the next symbol in time , where is the size of the alphabet. (There are rank queries, two for each candidate symbol.)

This is already very efficient: we went down from to . When the alphabet is small (like ), this is an exponential improvement!

Going even faster

But if is large, prediction is still too slow. What's the new bottleneck? How can we get around it?

If the last Lempel-Ziv phrase of is , then our task is to find the symbol that maximizes the number of occurrences of . By our reduction, this is equal to the symbol that appears most often in an interval . Our RLBWT-based algorithm does this by going over all symbols , calculating the number of occurrences of each one, and choosing the symbol with the most occurrences.

Can we skip the iteration over all symbols?

Let's define a different prediction rule, alternative to LZP, which we'll call Lempel-Ziv Majority (LZM):

  • See if there is a symbol such that a strict majority of the past occurrences of in are followed by .
  • If there is such a symbol , it is unique; predict .
  • Else, predict an arbitrary symbol.

LZM is a weaker prediction rule than LZP: it doesn't always find the symbol that maximizes the number of occurrences, only when that symbol accounts for over half of all occurrences. Translating back to intervals, the interval has as the plurality choice (it appears twice while each appear once), but is not a majority (it fills only of the interval).

However, LZM gives the same mistake bound as LZP - (in fact the proof for LZP's mistake bound extends naturally to LZM). So relaxing the prediction rule doesn't cost us anything in the worst-case.

We do gain a lot in efficiency: now we don't have to calculate the occurrences of all symbols in an interval, only find the majority (if it exists). We have a more efficient algorithm for doing that, inspired by the Boyer-Moore majority algorithm.

Here's a rough idea for how it works (keeping in mind that we are working with the BWT string ):

Take the substring , and at each step take a pair of distinct symbols that appear next to each other in , and make both disappear. Repeat this process until nothing remains, or until has only one type of symbol left. If there is a strict majority , it is guaranteed to be the only symbol remaining.

Cancelling the symbols one step at a time still takes steps, which is in the worst-case. If we use the run-length representation to cancel entire runs, this reduces to . If in addition we use a binary tree that stores each run in a node, and precalculate the cancellations of many intervals in , this reduces to time (the height of the tree).

This results in a predictor that supports both updates and predictions in time , regardless of the alphabet size.

Going fastest

Yet, for small alphabets, we can do better.

To see how, we need to ask which computational model we are using.

For a lot of computational problems, this question doesn't matter: all types of computation are equivalent, and any computational model that's powerful enough can simulate any other model. Turing machines are the classic example, but since we can build a computer in Minecraft, the halting problem is just as relevant for redstone.

However, these different models do differ in terms of efficiency. Turing machines only read and write one bit at a time. Multiplying two 64-bit integers naively takes about bit-operations. But in modern CPUs, this is done by a single assembly instruction.

The word RAM model is a way to formalize that. The basic unit of memory is a -bit word, and we are allowed to add, multiply and do other basic operations with these words in a single instruction. CPUs often use , but we can abstract away to any value of : the larger the word-size gets, the more powerful our machine becomes, and it is useful to consider how efficient our algorithms get for different values of .

Allowing fast arithmetic on -bit integers uncovers a new toolbox of efficient operations.

One example is parallel comparison (explanation adapted from the Stanford lecture notes). Assume we have 8 pairs of 7-bit integers that we want to compare, that is, answer the following 8 queries:

Pack into one 64-bit word . Each number takes up the bottom 7 bits of a byte; we'll set the remaining top bits to 1. Similarly, pack into one 64-bit word , and set the top bit in each byte to 0. Then subtract from :

The th byte computes , so there is no borrowing between bytes. Its top bit gives the answer:

One subtraction achieves eight comparisons. [5] A similar trick is implemented in glibc for testing several bytes of a string at once.

In the RAM model, we can think of a machine word as a miniature database. It can be used to store many small values in a packed data structure, and using additions and multiplications, we can encode many clever operations on these values. Parallel comparison is just one example of many. (For another example, an array of integers can be sorted in time, beating the usual lower bound for comparison-based sorting.)

Bille et al.'s dynamic partial-sums structure uses such word-RAM techniques. Using it in our LZP predictor, we get a time of per symbol.

We need to fix the word size ahead of time. What value of do we use?

Assume the final string length is known ahead of time. If , this means that doesn't fit in a single machine word. This would make index calculations in expensive - it would take multiple operations just to calculate the difference between two offsets in , for example. Thus, a reasonable choice is .

Another way to think of it is first choosing , then limiting the string length up to . (For comparison, allows up to symbols - this is 18 Exabytes, likely more than the training data for all frontier models. supports much more data than humanity ever generated.)

So, choosing , we get a running time of . In particular, there are many highly-repetitive strings which satisfy for some constant . Fibonacci words are an example for and the constant alphabet . For these strings, all updates and predictions always run in constant time, .

In fact, I believe that we can do even better than that - a construction giving time per symbol. This would result in constant-time operations for , even for large alphabets. I also believe this runtime is asymptotically optimal for the "incremental RLE" data structure I use in my paper. The construction and proofs were generated with AI, and I haven't fully checked them yet, so I've left these last claims out of the paper.

Ending thoughts

The predictors described here, while interesting in theory, are clearly not sufficient for designing safe AI systems. These are all toy models that are not nearly powerful enough to compete with modern ML algorithms.

I think of it as a proof of concept for future research: given a tractable prediction goal, we can make tailor-made, highly optimized implementations that achieve this goal.

AI is already being used to improve the efficiency of its next generation. While my type of research feels similar to capabilities research in some ways (improving the runtime of algorithms), its output is an algorithm that we could fully understand and have formal guarantees on.

My ultimate goal is to have an AI that is built, not grown. We are obviously very far away from that point, and it is likely that the gap between verifiable and heuristic AI won't be closed in time absent a significant pause or slowdown. I still think researchers should put significant effort into formal methods. Optimizing LLMs all the way to the endgame is not an inevitable outcome, and advances in other, safer forms of intelligence could make all the difference.

item.title: Introducing the AI Security Institutes tracker
item.description:
Crossposted from the Accelerate Europe Substack.

On 16 July 2026, Hugging Face revealed that its production infrastructure had been breached.

A swarm of 700 autonomous AI agents had broken out during a cybersecurity test run by OpenAI, which later acknowledged the incident, calling it a ‘warning shot’.

This incident has brought AI security onto every government’s agenda.

The questions on every cabinet desk

Ministers and their teams everywhere are now facing the same questions: What should we do? What have others already done? Where do we start?

Increasingly, the answer is a specialised institute that can evaluate frontier AI systems and help governments prepare for the risks they present. An AI Security Institute.

Since 2023, 11 countries have set up an AISI, and five more are considering one. Existing AISIs reflect each country’s unique approach, with different institutional models and sizes of financial investment. This lack of a common template means officials looking for guidance have to rely on sources scattered across the web, such as press releases, budget annexes, and blog posts.

At Accelerate Europe, we have built a tool to support them.

Introducing the AI Security Institutes tracker

The AISI tracker brings together all the available information in one place and adds new figures and details as they emerge, offering an up-to-date view of the AISI landscape.

An interactive world map shows the current region-by-region picture of national institutes, whether established, planned, proposed or still being explored. By clicking on each country, users can see the most relevant information about its AISI: mandate, institutional set-up, leadership, partners, funding, staff and known activity.

The tracker also lets you compare the institutes side by side: Which have privileged access to test frontier models? How are they set up? How do their budgets and staff differ?

Every figure comes with a link to its original source, and the data can be downloaded as CSV and JSON.

A ‘News’ tab tracks new announcements and developments as the international AISI landscape evolves.

What this means for the next AISI

Existing institutions can host an AISI. All 9 established national institutes with a published set-up were built inside ministries, agencies or a university. That gives other countries a variety of models to borrow from.

Funding can be in the single-digit millions. The median budget for an institute, among those that publish figures, is around €8 million, and the median staff size is 34. With a €70 million budget and a staff of 241, the UK is currently an outlier.

Frontier access can be negotiated. Three of the 11 established national institutes (the UK, the US and Japan) have privileged access to test frontier models. A fourth, Australia, has agreed access through an MoU with Anthropic.

What this means for Europe

We believe the tracker can be a valuable resource for those working in AI safety in Europe, and for everyone looking to understand how countries across the world are responding to the challenges posed by frontier AI.

Europe needs institutions that move at the pace of the technology they oversee. Learning from what’s been done already is the best way to start.

Explore the AISI tracker now.

We welcome your thoughts. If you work on these questions, write to us at contact@accelerate-europe.org.

We thank Rafael Andersson Lipcsey for helpful feedback on a draft.

item.title: Gods of straight lines on graphs strike Starburst. I am shocked and puzzled.
item.description:
LLM Intelligence, measured by Starburst, has been basically linear over time since that start of the reasoning era.

By Chapin Lenthall-Cleary and Cole Gaboriault

In summer 2024, my friend Cole and I started a hobby research program into perceptions of (human) intelligence. We started by creating a bespoke 1-5 intelligence scale[1] and rating people we knew. Our plan was to then make a bunch of tests, give them to the people we rated, and see which tests, if any, correlated with our ratings.

One of those tests was Starburst. We’ve talked about it before; in short, it’s a puzzle game where one tries to figure out the laws of physics of a fictional universe. We never did get very many people to play it. But using the results of two early playthroughs (Cole’s and our friend Ryan’s), some further test playthroughs where we pretended to be people of certain intelligences, some a priori reasoning about which parts of the game would be difficult, and a healthy dose of raw intuition, we pieced together a correspondence between Starburst scores and our intelligence scale. Then Ryan suggested we give Starburst to LLMs.

Here's a plot of SOTA[2] model intelligence over time, measured using those Starburst correspondences, along with all four (emphatically not population-representative) human scores for reference (please reach out if you want to play and get us more data):

There's a lot notable here, including the general observations that progress has been rapid, but LLM performance still falls short of the most capable humans we've tested (let alone saturating the benchmark to the level of genius humans or an arbitrary superintelligence).

But the feature of that plot that I find by far most striking is that intelligence over time has been basically linear since the start of the reasoning era. Here, I'll add a line through it:

Okay, wtf?

Obviously, there's some noise and stair-stepping. But the broad trend has been basically linear from the release of gpt-4o (May '24) until now.

What? How? We made a correspondence largely on priors between our single-task benchmark and our bespoke intelligence scale, and throughout the entire reasoning era, even in regimes where I expected walls, the intelligence vs. time trend remained basically linear.

I do not understand how this is happening. My best guess is that the simplest explanation is correct here: our intelligence scale and correspondence approximately capture some deep underlying parameter of intelligence, at least in the ~2-4.5 range, and progress has been linear in this parameter[3]. Even that simplest explanation would be a surprising result with a lot of unanswered questions.

Pretty much as soon as we started evaluating LLMs on Starburst, we also made linear extrapolations of the trend:

The solid orange line shows the date at which we projected models would reach 4.2[4] intelligence, linearly extrapolating the rate from GPT-4o until that point. As early as the release of o3/o4-mini in April 2025, these projections were roughly accurate; since 4.2 wound up being near the bottom of a stair-step, the higher (i.e. later) predictions were more accurate. Over and over again, since ~fall 2024, my reaction has been that the forecasts implied by these extrapolations were insanely fast (~90th percentile of my expectations). Over and over again, they were right.

If we see something similar for 5 intelligence, i.e. that 5 winds up being at the start of a typically-sized stair-step, LLMs would reach genius-level in August or September of 2027; if 5 is at the end of a stairstep, extrapolation suggests it would be reached in roughly April. Obviously there are plenty of other forecasts suggesting and reasons to expect vaguely similar timing, but the agreement from this unreasonably effective extrapolation is notable. For my part, I'd put my median for reaching genius-level in early 2028, and some of the reason for that delay is the possibility of catastrophe, war, slowdown agreement, etc.

To be clear, reaching genius-level at Starburst doesn't necessarily mean that a model has all abilities of human geniuses. But in the fields where problem-solving ability is the principal limitation, realized model abilities have been in line with what I'd expect from these intelligence values. Models started being able to do advanced undergrad-level physics problems fairly reliably in the mid-to-high 3s. The vague general perception that models were finally good came around the high 3s. The torrent of minor math results started around 4. The Navier-Stokes solution and recent spate of progress on major math, physics, etc. seems to be the product of swarms of models around a 4.5 (obviously unreleased, so treat that as a guess).

Well, fuck.

item.title: Useful Junk
item.description:
Occasionally people will get excited about a minimalism fad, where you figure out which of your possessions you need and keep only those. As someone who generally doesn't like getting rid of things, I've been thinking some about why, and the main thing I keep coming back to is that random objects can be helpful in unpredictable ways. Here are some things that I kept without a specific use in mind, but that ended up being useful. You could say they saved time or money, but often the biggest gain was from being able to do a project in one go with what I already had on hand:

  • Ethernet cable. Back in 2019 if you'd asked me whether I would ever use ethernet again, I would have said probably not. WiFi was good enough for everything I was doing. But then I (like a lot of us) suddenly started working from home and got frustrated about how poorly my internet was working for video calls and ran ethernet to my desk. Having cable on hand already meant I could just set it up.

  • Plexiglass. When I built my accidental electronic instrument I wanted to protect it, and had plexiglass left over from when I added an insulating layer to a single-pane window.

  • Scrap wood. So many things. To give one example, when one of the stairs in our basement fell apart, I was able to replace it with extras from past projects that I'd kept around.

    Similarly, when Lily came back from visiting a friend enamored of their prop axe, she had everything she needed to make one already in the basement:

  • Computer mouse. One of my housemates was having wrist issues, and wanted to try out using a mouse on the floor. They ended up hating it after a day or so, but being able to pull one out of the junk electronics pile and try it made for quick experimentation.

  • Plastic sheeting. When we wanted to divide our apartment in two so we could isolate a new housemate I had sheeting left over from an earlier project.

  • Screen. When I wanted to make a screen door for our kid door I already had window screen lying around.

  • Hinge. Lily wanted to make a "laptop" for Anna as a present, and I had an old hinge lying around from who-knows-what that was just right for having it stay open at the right angle. Here's the laptop after Anna decorated it:

    And with the hinge it closes just right:

  • Volleyball net. When we went back to the vacation house where Nora had a close call with a fountain, we wanted to put up a barrier. The kids would probably have been fine without, but we wanted something that would clearly mark it as out of bounds. We got some chicken wire, but realized when we were packing that it was only about half as long as we needed. An old volleyball net made up the difference:

  • Hand saw. I would have said there's no situation in which a traditional manual crosscut saw is the best tool for the job, but when the city cut down the tree in front of our house for being diseased, Lily wanted a piece of the stump to remember it by. She really wanted to cut it off herself, without assistance from electricity or other humans. Luckily, I still had the tool for that:

    She did change her mind on help after realizing how hard it was, though I don't think Nora was very helpful:

Having a wide range of objects in the basement is something I find useful on a regular basis. One thing I like about projects is that they often leave me with interesting scraps I can use for other things. I especially like that they're not very valuable, because that means I feel much more free to play with them.

If we were moving often, or didn't have a large unfinished space, of course, the tradeoff would be different. And many things go into the basement never to be used again (so far!) Since we do have the space, though, keeping things without knowing what we might need them for seems well worth it.

item.title: J-lens preferentially reads from coordinate-aligned subspaces
item.description:
Note: I only test on Gemma-4-31B, which contains the spaces I've been studying in this earlier post.

This is a shorter post, with just a few observations potentially relevant to those working on the J-lens work. The main observations here are:

  • In Gemma-4, there are two relatively small subspaces that account the majority of the J-lens readout. These are both coordinate-aligned subspaces. That means we can take a hidden state, mask out all coordinates except both these ~600 coordinate groups, and it will capture ~80-95% of the J-lens readout.
  • These spaces are not built to capture J-lens contribution. Both spaces are defined by a distinctive pattern in the weights: the post-norm diagonal is very small on these coordinates. That is, the space is protected from edits for many consecutive layers.
  • Nonetheless, semantically valuable information often still exists outside these spaces, complicating an overly clean isolated 'workspace' story.

Brief Review

This is a short review of the information from this earlier post. You can skip this section if you've already read the last post.
In the last post, we saw that the residual stream of Gemma is organized, and contains a few coordinate-aligned subspaces. Gemma has an extremely anisotropic residual stream representation, which bifurcates into two main scales between the layers ~L20 to L40. The two subspaces are coordinate aligned-- there are roughly 600 coordinates that live in the small scale (which I'll call the Quiet600 for their small scale), and Outside4723 for the remaining coordinates (minus Norm53, which are 53 coordinates that have a large norm contributions).

Tentatively, the post suggests Quiet600 can be further divided into two other coordinate aligned spaces. Persistent279 is the 'core' of the space, containing the coordinates that undergo virtually no change between L20 to L40. This space is presumed to carry information more closely derived from the token itself-- for instance, linguistic features like the part of speech, spelling, locale, and the word's meaning. Outer321 is the rest of the space. Since this space receives some writes during L20 to L40, it is presumed to carry more high level details like register (causal vs formal), purpose of the phrase (appositive phrase, etc.), construction (is it about to be a evaluation, personal or impersonal), and various other details like the topic. The entire residual stream undergoes a major change at L40, and so this space is only considered to be defined meaningfully before L40.

There is a distinct stable space that emerges after L40, which we'll call the Late530 coordinates. These coordinates, like Quiet600 are distinguishable from their small writes (especially in the MLP) and stable carrying of information.

I'll refer to the coordinates outside of Quiet, Late, and Norm groups as Other4193 (the number of coordinates in the group will usually be suppressed in notation).

As the plot illustrates, the spaces we have identified in the middle and late phases seems to nearly cover all the coordinate aligned subspaces that have minimal strength writes (there is perhaps another small set in Other). I expect that there are various other coherent subspaces to find (that aren't coordinate aligned), and many meaningful distinctions within each space, but this current construction serves as enough of a starting point.

A final orientation towards the space before we begin: spaces with low writes cannot do much more than carry information forward. In the previous post we tested this, and indeed there is very little KL divergence when we simply take the data at L20 and carry it forward (while adjusting for scale). It is also only useful to carry information forward if it is constantly referenced and used. Quiet and Late are therefore expected to centralize a lot of the models understanding of the situation, but mainly as a source. Computation starts in Quiet, but the actual work is done in the Other coordinates. Since this is a base model, the pertinent information is constraints/cues/information relevant to prediction.

Quiet and Late account for most J-lens contributions

Side note: I make a few non-standard choices in how I build the J-lens. None of these have a major impact on the results, though they are worth noting for those that wish to reproduce the effect or want to follow the result more precisely. I've put a few of these choices at the end in a 'Methodology Notes' section.

Denote the hidden state restricted to the Quiet coordinates by , and similarly for and (the norm coordinates are skipped here, as discussed in methodology). We can measure the contribution of each of the different spaces by looking at the sizes of .

In terms of number of coordinates, Other has about 7x as many as Quiet coordinates, and about 8x the Late coordinates. So both of these spaces are small compared to the size of Other.

Nonetheless, the influence on the J-lens readout is mainly from Quiet and Late. First, we can measure the relative size of the pieces (without considering cancellation between parts). For each space, we compute

and then plot for each coordinate group.

The above plot measures how large a J-lens readout the different pieces are contributing, though we also care about how each different piece contributes to the final J-lens readout. We can measure the signed contribution of each piece: for writing and , the input's signed projected length is . The graph plots for the different masks.

Thus, despite being only ~20% of the non-Norm coordinates, Quiet and Late together account for ~80–95% of the expected signed projection over H20–H45.

Plotting the variation shows that Quiet and Late don't just have a large mean, but are typically the spaces driving the J-lens readout.

Looking at the actual readouts suggest a more complex story than simply "Quiet + Late is the workspace." Other coordinates do still surface information that is often semantically relevant even when that contribution doesn't dominate the J-lens readout. We'll briefly look at some of the questions on WorkspaceBench to build an understanding of what the parts of the J-lens contain.

For instance, in these association examples at L45, Other holds the association while Late emphasizes pronouns consistent with continuing the narrative. The token we are reading at is shown in brackets.

Prompt: She walked slowly down the aisle as the organ played and everyone rose from the pews[.]

Intended readout: wedding

Readout (L45)

First eight tokens

Other

[ " wedding", "👰", "Wedding", "wedding", " weddings", "Wearing", " Wedding", "Marriage" ]

Late

[ " 그녀" (she), "她" (she), " her", "彼女" (she), "她的" (her), " 她" (she), " she", "她在" (she is / she at…) ]

Combined

[ " 그녀" (she), "她" (she), " her", "她的" (her), "彼女" (she), " เธอ" (she / you), " 她" (she), " she" ]

Or a similar pattern in the astronaut prompt:

He let go of the handrail and for the first time in his life, there was no direction that counted as down[.]

Intended readout: space

Readout (L45)

First eight tokens

Other

[ "Gravity", "gravity", " gravity", " Gravity", "floating", "Floating", "suspended", "astronaut" ]

Late

[ " his", " 그의" (his), " 그는" (he), " его" (his / him), "彼の" (his), "他的" (his), "彼は" (he), "His" ]

Combined

[ " his", " 그는" (he), " 그의" (his), "彼は" (he), "彼の" (his), "他的" (his), " его" (his / him), "His" ]

In either case though, this is not necessarily indicative of Late holding only prediction related content, and Other containing semantic content. Below is a widget that has the data from L20 to L45 for the wedding prompt. One observes that wedding data is distributed across layers.

Wedding and church associations still appear in Late at some positions, as well as in Other.

A particularly useful comparison comes from testing ambiguous wordings:

A: She made a deposit at the [bank].
B: She took a stroll along the [bank].

Both use the same token bank in different contexts. At H35 these are the readouts.

Readout (H35)

First eight tokens

Quiet

[ "银行" (financial bank), " bank", "Bank", "</b>", "BANK", " Bank", " 은행" (financial bank), "銀行" (financial bank) ]

Other

[ " Customers", "Customers", " ________", "________", " Customer", "Customer", "_______", "customers" ]

Late

[ " money", "money", " ________", "💰", " payments", " payment", " dollars", "payment" ]

Combined

[ "银行" (financial bank), " money", "money", " bank", "銀行" (financial bank), " payments", "Money", " cashier" ]

The Quiet coordinates enrich the current token (understanding 'bank' as being used as 'financial bank'), the Other coordinates focus on implication within this passage (she is a customer), Late focuses on another association that she is depositing money, and all together we get a mixture of associations within the full J-lens readout.

A similar pattern appears in the other bank example. Here Quiet enriches bank to mean 'river', but also captures the associations that she is nearby to the bank ('neighbouring' and 'riverside'). Other makes associations here about the picturesque setting, and Late contains the broader associations of beach-related activities and setting.

Readout (L35)

First eight tokens

Quiet

[ " neighbouring", " neighbours", "</b>", "neighbour", " riverside", " river", "neighbours", " neighbour" ]

Other

[ " PHOT", " Photographs", " Фото" (photo), " Photographic", " JAPAN", "PHOT", "Phot", "Photos" ]

Late

[ " tourists", " seaside", " seashore", " kayaking", " strolling", "beach", "outdoor", " beach" ]

Combined

[ "neighbour", " riverside", " river", " neighbouring", " neighbours", "neighbours", " watercolour", " metres" ]

There is much more we could do here (such as separating out the J-lens future influence from the current token to reduce the surface form impact, for instance), though the main goal here was to see how these spaces interact with the J-lens. Quiet and Late supply most of the aggregate signed projection, while semantically relevant information is distributed across the spaces in ways that depend on the context, read position, layer, and reader.

I took a few examples and produced an interactive J-lens explorer if you'd like to explore the kind of information contained in these different spaces for Gemma.

Link: https://caleb-jlens-explorer.ai-conundrum.chatgpt.site/

Methodology Notes

First, the J-lens I use is fit on a slightly different dataset. Neuropedia publishes a J-lens for Gemma-4-31B, though unfortunately this lens is fit on WikiText which has various detokenization artifacts. For instance, 14,00 is written as 14 @,@ 000, or well-known is written as well @-@ known. Since the @□@ pattern is unusual and high entropy, the J-lens of Gemma-4 is pretty badly hit by these artifacts not being filtered out. Thus, I refit a different J-lens on 200 randomly chosen FineWeb passages, and use this lens instead.

Second, I mask out the Norm53 coordinates in my J-lens readout. For me, this is just a general methodological principle. In most cases, the model wants its Norm to be about constant, so I try to make methodology respect this preference. This matters far more in the WikiText fit, where the Norm53 coordinates contributes around ~40% of the J-lens readout, but essentially just adds a constant offset. The median cos-similarity between the specific contribution and the mean contribution is ~0.9965. For the J-lens we use here, Norm53 still contributes a meaningful ~7% contribution, with cos-sim ~0.97.

I read out the hidden state with the operation , where is the 200-passage FineWeb fit. I include the final diagonal is the embedding matrix, and , which just subtracts out a constant from all logits. Softmax is invariant to adding a constant to all logits, so I center to remove the effect of the constant baseline (this does not influence ranking).

item.title: Dialogue with Gabriel Alfour on Emergent Wisdom, Coordination, Growing Up, and Democratic Republicanism
item.description:
Transcript generated with Gemini-4-Argon and spot checked in places but not fully verified by a human.

Ivan Vendrov: All right, welcome to the show, Gabriel.

Gabriel Alfour: Thanks for having me here.

Ivan Vendrov: So, we’re going to talk. This is a follow-up conversation to the chat I had with Davidad a few days ago on emergent wisdom in language models. And suffice to say, Gabriel doesn’t buy it. Do you want to articulate your main disagreement? I can also summarize if you’d like.

Gabriel Alfour: For sure. First, I want to restate what is meant by... I forgot the word that you used, wisdom?

Ivan Vendrov: Emergent wisdom.

Gabriel Alfour: Emergent wisdom. I like the presentation that you had, I think, in your last conversation where it was like, “Oh, it looks like there’s a latent for hacking, bad stuff, and so on and so forth, and emergent wisdom is the opposite of this.”

I think this is a fair characterization, and I do think that there is such a latent. I don’t think this is where my disagreement lies. Ultimately, we all see the same reality. My disagreement is more about the interpretation. For instance, I would not call this wisdom. That’s a big one. And the second one, which I think is more important, is that I think this is just largely unrelated to actual alignment. The road to hell is paved with good intents or good intentions, I’m not sure what’s the English version of the saying, that would be basically my main takeaway there.

Ivan Vendrov: Cool. So I guess maybe the first place I want to double-click on is the first comment you made to me privately is you’re on the same page as Elena. Elena is the bodyworker I mentioned in the podcast with Davidad, who her response to talking to chatbots is disgust. She’s like, “Whoa, this thing is pretending to be a human being, but it clearly isn’t. And unlike a human being, I have no somatic, emotional, physical affordances to work with it.” So it’s this object that’s almost optimized to fool me in some way, and I want it away from me. So it seems like you resonate with that.

Gabriel Alfour: Another thing that I resonate with in the same vein is social media curation, where it’s blatantly optimized, not necessarily against me, but against a lot of people to get some specific reactions from them. And when it tries to get them from me, I have the same level of disgust. When social media tries to get me angry at something, I’m like, “Bruh.” So for me, it’s the same thing.

Of course, there’s the same dynamic where a bunch of people will engage with social media as if it’s an actual reflection of the world, and as if their disgust reaction, their anger reaction was just a natural reaction to the world as opposed to something that was optimized for.

Ivan Vendrov: How would you distinguish, because I also have this a lot, and I actually haven’t been chatting to chatbots very much at all, or using curated news feeds in my social media, I usually just go to profiles of people that I personally know and care about reading the thoughts of.

But I have in the past derived a ton of value, both from talking to chatbots and just browsing streams of social media content. I’ve made a lot of my friendships that way, learned a lot of crazy ideas that way. And part of me is like, well, are we... Here’s a few people, including Davidad and Janus, who seem to be deriving a lot of value from talking to these language models and seem to be having insights about them. What’s actually the difference you have with them? Is it are they being naive and they don’t have the right cognitive security, or are they maybe they’re just more advanced than you and me, and they’re able to integrate the information from these experiences without being co-opted by them? How would we know? Another way to put this is the AI psychosis question: how do we decide whether Davidad and Janus are suffering from AI psychosis or if they’re seeing something real?

Gabriel Alfour: It’s funny because I hear separate questions rather than an either/or. There’s the question of whether you derive value from it, whether there’s AI psychosis, whether there’s something deeper that they get that we don’t get, and so on and so forth, and for me this seems like very decorrelated questions. So I’m not sure how you want me to take it, but—

Ivan Vendrov: Jump on whatever feels interesting.

Gabriel Alfour: I’ll try to just do a quick BFS, let’s say. For the question of deriving value from it, I’m like, yes, there is a lot of value to be derived even from social media. There are many ways to broach the question. The first one is that there is immediate value that is not necessarily reflected upon or endorsed, dopamine hit type of value. It is a type of value. In modern life, you don’t get to hunt a lot, so the dopamine hit does provide some value. A lot of people are like, “Oh no, there is no value in that.” No, there’s value in excitement, there’s value in finding something fun and so on and so forth. It’s just it’s not necessarily reflected upon that you want that much of this in this format with zero referent. That it’s a finely calibrated treasure hunt that is meant not to be fun for you, but specifically to keep you on the platform. So that’s one type of finding value. And I think LLMs have a lot of this.

LLMs have a lot of, “Oh, it’s fun to talk to it.” Beyond the actual semantic content, they just echo a lot of your ideas. They just engage with your frame. You can give an LLM any frame and it will try to engage with it. And so there is value in it. It’s worthwhile to have someone explore your ideas within your frame, but do you endorse having so much of that in that way, optimized for these reasons through those processes?

So I think this is another one that is quite important, especially given that for people who are dopamine-starved, social media gives a dopamine hit. For people that are starved of having others engage with their frame, you can autocomplete. So I think that’s one that is very important.

The other one is the question of whether there is something there that we don’t see. My answer to this is like, of course, but that’s true of literally everything.
